work.full: Design for Dasein: Understanding the Design of Experiences
work.author: Thomas Wendt

role: Foundational phenomenology chapter; serves as an interpretive DESIGN LENS (Dasein, ready-to-hand/present-at-hand, coping, breakdown, standing reserve, thing-ness) for reading the design of experiences. Reports Wendt only; RO mapping not built here.

sections.title: Dasein is a Design Process (intro: Heidegger vs. Husserl; mundane-ifying philosophy)
Dasein and the situated-ness of Being; 'in' as involvement not containment (airport context example)
Being ahead of itself (future-directedness; Stiegler 'not yet'); thrownness and coping; design as un-throwing
Beckett's Malone Dies as Dasein-being-involved-in-objects; 'our objects define us'
Connecting the Poles of Self and World (rejecting Cartesian dualism; embodied cognition; to-do apps; dualism in design)
Praxis and Situated Action (theory vs. practical action; acting-on vs acting-through; knowing-that vs knowing-how; praxis = theory-informed practice; sketching)
Interaction Patterns (the tool analysis: Vorhandenheit/present-at-hand & Zuhandenheit/ready-to-hand; continuum; withdrawal; Dourish's mouse)

Reflecting on the Object Experience (Malone redux; nearness as orientation; usability & social learning; Dreyfus coping; breakdown/Bonsiepe; abandonment; conspicuousness; meaning/Krippendorff; Taylorism critique)
Heidegger on Technology (technē/poiēsis/physis; das Entbergen bringing-forth; Herausfordern challenging-forth; standing reserve/Bestand; enframing/Gestell; The Turn)
Making Sense of Technology (default phenomenological stance; making sense/Krippendorff; care; equipmental whole; object vs thing — the jug; thing-ness via meaning-gathering; designer's becoming)

key_terms.gloss: Da (here/there) + Sein (being) = being-there / being-in-the-world; situated, embodied Being that is not an abstract form explaining our state but the embodied state itself; distinctive in that its own being is an issue for it (self-conscious, anxious).
The 'in' is not Aristotelian spatial containment but involvement/absorption; human and world are one entity resulting from Dasein's engaged involvement in an undifferentiated world.
Dasein is future-directed: all current focus is directed toward future goals; Stiegler's 'having-to-be', existence extending (Erstreckung) between 'already' and 'not yet'.
Geworfenheit; Dasein is dropped into a non-ideal world it must cope with; design = 'un-throwing' (Dutch ontwerpen), making order out of chaos, deciding form to liberate us from life's arbitrariness.

Dealing with the world by interacting with things; both handling broken/non-optimal situations and the ordinary incorporation of things into life; default mode of being (after Dreyfus), representation-free.
Descartes' mind-over-body split; the 'I'/mind as wholly distinct from the body; rejected by phenomenology and identified as the root of design's theory/practice and thinking/doing splits.
Groundwork laid by dissolving self/world: environment as extension of mind, things as extensions of bodies; the inner/outer distinction vanishes in absorbed coping.

Theoretically-informed practice; takes the rigor of theory and embeds it into practical action; in the Aristotelian sense, action-over-making, emphasis on the process itself rather than the final product.
Acting upon takes the object itself as focal point; acting through takes the user's end goal as focal point (object recedes).
Dreyfus via the hammer: understanding a hammer most primordially means knowing how to hammer, not knowing that it has certain properties.
Object as tool for a goal, an extension of the body; user acts through it; it withdraws/fades into the background as a transparent means; 'equipmentality' = transparency w.r.t. user intention.

Object observed as wholly separate, factual, analyzable from afar; decontextualized, detached speculation; the mode entered when smooth interaction breaks and the object becomes an object of deliberation.
In the ready-to-hand mode the object disappears from view; 'the ready-to-hand is not grasped theoretically at all'; our dealings dwell with the work, not the tools.
Mode of being when acting through ready-to-hand technology: action without conscious thought, caught up in the performance of the work (Dourish/Dreyfus); examples: jazz musicians, carpenters.

Rupture of smooth coping (Bonsiepe/Krippendorff/Dreyfus); not a negative to avoid but reveals 'the tissue of the relations' needed for tasks; what breaks down is the meaningfulness of the interface, not the artifact.
When equipment malfunctions it becomes 'conspicuous' (Heidegger); instruments shift from embodied to disembodied/present-at-hand objects.
Near/far concern the orientation of Dasein, not physical space; an object is near to the extent it is part of the user's current orientation/use; clothing can be physically near yet 'praxically far'.
Dasein's key attribute; it is concerned with surrounding things and finds its own meaning in them; without a means to manifest itself Dasein fades into the background.

The nearest things ('equipment') given as a unity that varies in range (expanding/contracting), visible only 'in excerpts'; experienced rather than analyzed; framing our view turns objects into things.

A self-supporting thing 'differs from an object'; it becomes an object only when placed before us in perception/representation; thingness lies not in material but, for the jug, 'in the void that it holds'.

Determined by our ability to make sense of an object; active, ready-to-hand engagement carries us beyond object-ness into thing-ness; bringing-close/gathering creates a thing; the mobile device's thing-ness is given by its users.
The natural form/shape arising out of itself; 'form without intervention'; opposed to technē.
To make something appear through art, craft, the work of the hands; requires human intervention; the intentional act of making something appear; the practical side of poiēsis; that which reveals.

Bringing-forth; the poetical mode in which meaning emerges out of a pre-existing state; the poet/artist finds and extracts meaningful points rather than imposing meaning; art as hermeneutics of the world.

Not anything technological; 'all that is merely technological never arrives at the essence of technology'; per Rutsky a dynamic ongoing process/movement, not a static category; critique of instrumentalism.
Literally bringing-forth what was safely hidden (ent- = forth/out/negation; bergen = rescue/keep safe through concealment); the concealment/unconcealment, veiled/unveiled trope (Harman).
Modern technology's revealing as a 'challenging' that demands nature supply extractable, storable energy; connotes provocation/defiance; defies poiēsis; 'de-worlds' materials (chalice vs Rhine dam).

'Resource well'/'stock'; a pool of technological energy on call; whatever stands by as standing-reserve no longer stands over against us as object; the smartphone in the pocket; places the user in a passive position.
Our relationship with modern technology as the gathering of technologically stored energy as it reveals itself; the onus on designers to design responsibly and preserve the user–system relationship.
The shift between early (object-focused) and late (pseudo-Platonic, essence-of-technology) Heidegger that many scholars note; relevant to the apparent tension with the early tool analysis.
Wendt's claim that contemporary philosophy of technology and design — narrowing from poiēsis to everyday things veiled by ubiquity — is effectively taking a phenomenological stance.

claims.text: Heidegger shifts philosophy from theoretical formulations toward the everyday interactions of bodily entities, 'mundane-ifying' philosophy by asking the most universal/emptiest question — the meaning of Being.
Dasein is situated, embodied Being — not an abstract form explaining our embodied state but that state itself; the 'in' of being-in-the-world is involvement, not spatial containment.
Designers must read user context as involvement in a situation rather than physical location; the same place carries different concerns at different times (airport security vs. post-security).

The world reveals itself only when Dasein manipulates it; the designer's goal is to understand users' involvement as meaningful activity, attending to meaning derived, not only actions taken — else interaction is 'pantomime'.

Dasein is always ahead of itself (future-directed); everything designed should keep the end user's future goals in mind, since users interact to accomplish 'something less tangible', not for interaction's sake.
Dasein is thrown into a non-ideal world and copes by altering it from non-preferable to preferable; this altering is what links design to Dasein, and incorporation of things necessitates design.

Objects let Dasein 'play itself out' (Beckett's Malone); without their cluster of affordances we design our situations by substandard means — 'our objects define us… they shape our understanding of the world'.
Heidegger's attack on Cartesian dualism dissolves the self/world and mind/body splits — self and world are one entity, Dasein — laying the groundwork for embodied cognition.
Cartesian dualism pervades design; the theory/practice and thinking/doing splits are direct results of Cartesian thinking and misrepresent how design actually works (no clean phases).

Pure theory has less influence on how we interpret the world than practical action; an object's essential qualities are the actions it allows, not its physical properties — 'we know something by what we do with it'.

Praxis is theoretically-informed practice; in the Aristotelian sense it emphasizes process over product (action over making), exemplified by sketching as externalized thought, and decreases the compulsive need for immediate finality.

Ready-to-hand and present-at-hand are two poles of interaction on a continuum, not a binary; in the ready-to-hand mode the object withdraws and becomes a transparent means (equipmentality = transparency to user intention).

Interruptions inevitably shift interaction from ready-to-hand to present-at-hand; breakage is unavoidable, so the key design concern is how users cope with the breaks, and designing for that movement is the job of experience designers.

Things have no properties in themselves but only in relation to context of use (the failed hammer is 'too heavy' only as used by me); user testing should observe and design from coping strategies rather than eliminating 'unintuitive' aspects.

Breakdown is a necessary accompaniment to design that reveals the tissue of relations needed for tasks (Bonsiepe); the design target is to anticipate forms of breakdown and open up possibilities for action.

What breaks down is the meaningfulness of the interface, not the artifact (Krippendorff); products are abandoned when they become meaningless, not merely when usability is sub-par, so usability must be reconceived around meaning and confidence to handle disruption.

Modern technology is a 'challenging-forth' (Herausfordern) that demands nature supply extractable, storable energy and 'de-worlds' materials, unlike the bringing-forth (poiēsis) of craft; this is Heidegger's 'Turn' toward a non-instrumental, near-Platonic essence of technology.

The standing reserve (Bestand) places the user in a passive position; the 'invisible'/'intuitive' interface fantasy instantiates it, and enframing (Gestell) names our resulting relationship to technology — putting the onus on designers to design responsibly and preserve the user–system relationship.

An object becomes a thing only through active, ready-to-hand engagement that gathers meaning into it (the device's thing-ness is given by its users, not its material — 'the void that it holds'); thing-ness lies in the space of meaning, not physical attributes.

By neglecting the thing, philosophy has failed to address the nature of making; designers and philosophers should examine the thing in the process of designing/making — the 'becoming' that gathers material and meaning into a thing, and the gap between encoded meaning and users' actual behaviors.

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.work: Being and Time; The Question Concerning Technology
interlocutors.draws: Backbone of the chapter: Dasein, being-in-the-world as involvement, ahead-of-itself, thrownness, critique of Cartesianism, the tool analysis (ready-to-hand/present-at-hand, withdrawal, conspicuousness), care, equipmental whole, object/thing (the jug), and later technology themes (technē/poiēsis/physis, das Entbergen, Herausfordern, standing reserve/Bestand, enframing/Gestell, The Turn).

interlocutors.name: Edmund Husserl
interlocutors.draws: Named as Heidegger's teacher/foil; the subject–object split and theoretical phenomenology that Heidegger reacts against.

interlocutors.name: René Descartes
interlocutors.draws: Primary antagonist; the cogito and mind-over-body dualism (the 'I' wholly distinct from the body) diagnosed as the source of design's theory/practice and thinking/doing splits.

interlocutors.name: Hubert Dreyfus
interlocutors.work: What Computers Still Can't Do; commentary on Being and Time
interlocutors.draws: Knowing-that vs knowing-how (the hammer); critique of rule-based Cartesian AI; and especially practical coping as representation-free, skillful dealing with the world and technology.

interlocutors.name: Paul Dourish
interlocutors.draws: The 'how does the world reveal itself to us' reframing, and the lucid mouse example of ready-to-hand withdrawal vs. present-at-hand interruption.

interlocutors.name: Klaus Krippendorff
interlocutors.draws: Breakdown as loss of the meaningfulness of the interface; user-friendliness as confidence to handle disruption; Taylorism critique of functionalist usability; meaning as the sum of imaginable contexts; the paradox of making sense.

interlocutors.name: Gui Bonsiepe
interlocutors.draws: Breakdown as a necessary accompaniment to design that reveals the tissue of relations; design target = anticipate breakdowns and open possibilities for action.

interlocutors.name: Bernard Stiegler
interlocutors.draws: Dasein as 'having-to-be', existence extending (Erstreckung) between 'already' and 'not yet'.

interlocutors.name: Cameron Tonkinwise
interlocutors.draws: User testing as a social learning process; Apple's generational product education (iPod→iPhone→iPad).

interlocutors.name: Samuel Beckett
interlocutors.draws: Extended literary illustration of Dasein-being-involved-in-objects; objects as bodily extensions and loci of ambivalent care.

interlocutors.name: Graham Harman
interlocutors.draws: The concealment/unconcealment (veiled/unveiled) trope in Heidegger's das Entbergen.

interlocutors.name: R. L. Rutsky
interlocutors.draws: The 'essence of technology' as a dynamic ongoing process/movement, not a static category; broadening technology toward making/producing incl. artistic production.

interlocutors.name: Mark Weiser
interlocutors.draws: 'Calm computing' as the (unrealized) promise behind the 'invisible interface' and standing-reserve discourse.

interlocutors.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
interlocutors.draws: Invoked once via the design-as-thrownness gloss ('a throw of the dice on the table of the gods').

design_principles.name: Context-as-involvement
design_principles.gloss: Design for users' involvement in a situation, not merely their physical location; the same place carries different concerns at different times.

design_principles.name: Design for future goals
design_principles.gloss: Keep the end user's future goals in mind; users act to accomplish 'something less tangible', not to interact for its own sake.

design_principles.name: Praxis over premature finality
design_principles.gloss: Use prototypes/unfinished artifacts to test theory-laden assumptions in real use contexts; sketching as externalized thought; value action/process over making.

design_principles.name: Acting-through, not acting-on
design_principles.gloss: Center the user's end goal so the object/technology withdraws, rather than centering the object itself.

design_principles.name: Design for the ready-to-hand/present-at-hand continuum
design_principles.gloss: Design for the constant movement between absorbed coping and conscious deliberation; breakage is inevitable, so support coping with the shift.

design_principles.name: Design for coping, breakdown, and meaning
design_principles.gloss: Treat breakdown as revelatory; anticipate its forms and open possibilities for action; reconceive usability around meaning and confidence-to-handle-disruption, not functionalist (Taylorist) error-elimination.

design_principles.name: Responsible design against passive enframing
design_principles.gloss: Resist the 'invisible'/'intuitive'-interface fantasy and standing-reserve passivity; preserve an active user–system relationship.

design_principles.name: Design for thing-ness and imaginable contexts
design_principles.gloss: Support the user's meaning-gathering that turns objects into things; design for the full range of imaginable use contexts; mind the gap between encoded meaning and users' actual behaviors.

RO-hook: near an Aristotelian praxis/poiēsis distinction Wendt himself flags as 'the Aristotelian sense'.
RO-hook: candidate analogue for engaged actualization vs. reflective interruption.
RO-hook: candidate link to a meaning/desire telos.

ro_hooks.concept: standing reserve and the passive user
ro_hooks.note: RO-hook: active/passive axis as counter-point to an actualization-of-desire account foregrounding active engagement.

ro_hooks.concept: user-completed thing-ness; 'ward-off boredom' as a canonical use case
ro_hooks.note: RO-hook: candidate touch-point for the dissertation's boredom/engagement axis and an actualization-of-desire reading.
